figures.prompt:
Use case: infographic-diagram. Create one finished scientific infographic for a research preprint, landscape 16:9, high resolution, ideally 3840 x 2160. It will also be used as a standalone slide. Original new image; no reference image. Style: clean editorial scientific illustration with precise, flat vector-like linework, ample whitespace, warm white background (#FBFCFA), deep navy text (#12333E), teal (#087F8C), restrained amber (#D99A25), pale teal and pale amber fills. No gradients, textures, dark panels, decorative ornaments, watermark, or invented data. Large, very readable sans-serif typography; limit text to the exact copy below. Match a coherent three-figure series.

Title at top: 'Four questions about form'. Under it place two modest, separate horizontal interpretive boxes, clearly grouped under the small label 'THEORETICAL LENSES'. Left box: 'Wolfram: ruliad' and 'All possible computations'. Right box: 'Levin: Platonic space' and 'Proposed space of patterns'. Beneath the pair, a small centered line: 'Motivate questions; not tested here'. These are distinct philosophical proposals: do not merge the boxes or draw causal arrows from an abstract realm into matter.

Main visual: four equally weighted columns with large simple scientific diagrams, thin vertical separators, no connecting arrows between columns. Each column has an uppercase heading, one question, its diagram, and one short role label. Column 1: heading 'POSSIBILITY'; question 'What can exist?'; diagram a small branching network of alternative allowed configurations beside a rule-table icon; role label 'Rules'. Column 2: heading 'ACCESSIBILITY'; question 'What can be reached?'; diagram a schematic two-basin landscape with one teal trajectory entering a basin, no axes or quantitative scale; role label 'Body + history + resources'. Column 3: heading 'RECOGNITION'; question 'What counts as the same form?'; diagram the same small tiled pattern viewed through coarse and fine measurement grids, with an observer/lens icon outside the modeled object; role label 'Observer + scale'. Column 4: heading 'CONTINUATION'; question 'What keeps it available?'; diagram a simple loop between a tissue-grid icon labeled 'Body' and a small record-card icon labeled 'Record', with the record-to-body arrow labeled 'read' and the body-to-record arrow labeled 'write'; role label 'Body + record + reader'. Keep each arrow direction and label unambiguous.

Bottom takeaway, large and legible: 'Embodiment makes possibilities accessible and maintainable.' Small secondary line: 'Schematic framework, not a measured map of all forms.' Use only the quoted visible text. The four questions are analytical distinctions, not four chronological stages. Scientific simplicity and print legibility are more important than decorative complexity. Keep all labels inside generous margins.

Use case: infographic-diagram. Create one finished scientific infographic for a research preprint, landscape 16:9, high resolution, ideally 3840 x 2160. It will also be used as a standalone slide. Original new image; no reference image. Style: clean editorial scientific illustration with precise, flat vector-like linework, ample whitespace, warm white background (#FBFCFA), deep navy text (#12333E), teal (#087F8C), restrained amber (#D99A25), pale teal and pale amber fills. No gradients, textures, dark panels, decoration, watermark, or invented plots. Large readable sans-serif typography; match a coherent three-figure series.

Title: 'Three tests of pattern continuity'. Subtitle: 'Selected simulation results; different mechanisms'. Three horizontal panels separated by thin light-grey vertical rules. Give the first panel slightly more width, and keep every label large enough to read when printed across a journal page.

Left panel heading: 'A  REHOMING'. Secondary label: 'Strict-eight'. Diagram: a grey old-anchor disc at left labeled 'Old anchor', then a small amber break slash on a dashed trajectory, followed by an ellipsis representing a strictly later time, then exactly EIGHT teal daughter discs in one single horizontal followed-lineage chain. Number these eight discs 1 through 8. Keep all eight inside a single pale teal coherence enclosure; a bracket beneath all eight denotes the whole window. A light mesh beneath the row can suggest comparisons among all daughter pairs without obscuring the sequence. Do not draw a branching family or a binary tree. Visible lines below: '8 inherited daughters' and 'All 28 pairs coherent' and 'Each distinct from the old anchor'. Small status line: 'A finite lineage event'. No similarity thresholds or quantitative axes inside the artwork.

Middle panel heading: 'B  REPAIR'. Diagram: a small tissue grid labeled 'Body' and a partially damaged record-card labeled 'Record'. Show a two-way feedback loop: record-to-body arrow 'read', body-to-record arrow 'write'. From the resulting record, a separate arrow leads to a fresh tissue grid labeled 'Fresh-body assay'. Use one amber disruption mark to show damage, but keep some original record content and body structure visible. Visible explanation: 'Surviving body structure improves record repair'. Small status line: 'One repair episode'. Do not imply that the body is the sole information source, and do not draw an infinite repair loop or show invented before/after scores.

Right panel heading: 'C  RENEWAL'. Diagram: a small encoded record leads into a fresh cellular-automaton grid; its resulting activity writes a new record; a dashed vertical boundary separates this from the next fresh grid. Diagram labels only: 'Record', 'Fresh body', 'Rewrite', 'Next body'. The old body does not cross the replacement boundary. Visible result lines: 'CA: 64-bit payload, 16 generations' and 'Shared reading and writing machinery'. Beneath, a small amber contrast strip: 'L17 tissue loop: information declines'. Small status line: 'Renewal depends on architecture'. Do not depict 64 bits as an autonomous organism, and do not draw comparative bar charts or synthetic trajectories.

Bottom takeaway in large navy text: 'Coherence, repair and renewal are different claims.' Small secondary line: 'Schematic mechanisms; see captions for protocols and controls.' Use only the quoted visible text, with generous margins. This is a scientifically bounded explanatory diagram, not raw experimental data.

Use case: infographic-diagram. Create one finished scientific infographic for a research preprint, landscape 16:9, high resolution, ideally 3840 x 2160. It will also be used as a standalone slide. Original new image; no reference image. Style: clean editorial scientific illustration with precise, flat vector-like linework, ample whitespace, warm white background (#FBFCFA), deep navy text (#12333E), teal (#087F8C), restrained amber (#D99A25), pale teal and pale amber fills. No gradients, textures, dark panels, decorative ornament, watermark, or invented measured data. Large readable sans-serif typography; match a coherent three-figure series.

Title: 'From cell state to collective capacity'. Subtitle: 'Biological connections and the next scientific question'. Three large equally weighted panels across the canvas, with clear status badges and generous spacing. Do not connect the panels with a causal or inevitable-progress arrow.

Left panel status badge: 'BIOLOGICAL PRECEDENT'. Heading: 'Cell state'. Main diagram: one scientific cell outline with a nucleus and a simple internal feedback loop, a brief incoming exposure arrow, and an outgoing path to a later cell state. This is a generic schematic, not a micrograph or a literal identified molecular pathway. Labels: 'Exposure', 'Retained state', 'Later response'. Main explanatory line: 'History can change what a cell later restores.'

Middle panel status badge: 'DEMONSTRATED IN A MODEL'. Heading: 'Collective state'. Main diagram: a row of three teal donor cells communicating across a visible boundary with a row of three pale recipient cells, followed by a compact second snapshot where the old donors are greyed out and separated, while the three recipients are teal. A clear communication arrow joins the interacting groups; it does not connect separated donors to recipients after removal. Diagram labels: 'Contact', 'Donors removed', 'State retained'. Below, a prominent label: '12 carrier replacements'. Explanatory line: 'Communication passes state to new cells.' Small status line: 'Cells and schedule supplied'. This depicts a finite computational relay, not a clinical result or autonomous cell division.

Right panel status badge in amber: 'OPEN HYPOTHESIS'. Heading: 'Collective capacity'. Use a thin dashed amber panel outline to reinforce hypothetical status. Main diagram: a small network of six or seven interacting cell outlines arranged around a simple gap or obstruction. One route has an amber interruption cross; an alternative teal route passes through other members to the same small destination marker. The diagram illustrates possible flexible coordination, not an observed outcome. Diagram labels: 'Disruption', 'New roles', 'Same function'. Main questions: 'Can a group preserve function by changing roles?' and 'Can new members inherit that capacity?'

Bottom takeaway in large navy text: 'Shared state is established in a model; flexible collective goals remain open.' Small secondary line: 'Biological parallels motivate tests; they do not establish treatments.' Use only the quoted visible text. Keep status distinctions conspicuous and diagrams simple enough for scientific print reproduction.
